query: For CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys (X = Si, Mn, or Al) in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain whether a stable, coherent protective oxide layer forms and persists during exposure above 900 °C in an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere, rather than developing unstable surface oxides that crack or spall? Specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison against a defined baseline, the predicted differences, the applicable exposure and material-state boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a falsifying observation.

generation.hypothesis: In CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys, the ability to form and maintain a stable, coherent protective oxide scale above 900 °C is governed by the oxidation and diffusion behavior of the substituent element X. When X is Al or Si, the alloy forms slow-growing, thermodynamically stable oxides (Al2O3 or SiO2, possibly with contributions from Cr2O3) that yield a coherent, adherent barrier; in contrast, when X is Mn, faster diffusion and the formation of less stable, volatile oxides leads to scales that crack and spall.
generation.material_initial_state: CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloy in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state, with X = Al, Si, or Mn
generation.intervention: Exposure of the alloy to a controlled oxidative or corrosive atmosphere at temperatures above 900 °C
generation.conditions: Isothermal high-temperature exposure (e.g., 900–1100 °C) for extended durations (tens of hours) under controlled atmospheric conditions, with all samples prepared to have comparable homogeneous microstructures
generation.structural_mediator: The nature and continuity of the surface oxide scale, which is mediated by the diffusion rates and oxidation kinetics of the X element (and associated elements such as Cr) at the alloy surface
generation.mechanism: Al or Si in the alloy slow outward diffusion and react to form thermodynamically stable oxides (Al2O3 or SiO2) – possibly in combination with Cr2O3 – that minimize interfacial strain and stress, resulting in a continuous and coherent oxide layer that protects the substrate. In contrast, Mn promotes rapid diffusion (especially of Cr), leading to the formation of less adherent, rapidly growing oxides that develop internal stresses, crack, and spall away.
generation.predicted_outcome: Alloys with X = Al or Si will exhibit thin, slow-growing, coherent, and adherent oxide scales with relatively low mass gains and minimal spallation, whereas alloys with X = Mn will develop thicker, irregular oxide scales prone to cracking and spallation under identical conditions.
generation.baseline: The performance of CrFeCoNiMn alloys under the same high-temperature oxidative/corrosive conditions, which are predicted to form unstable, spalling oxide scales
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to single- or multiphase solid-solution CrFeCoNiX alloys exposed to temperatures above 900 °C in oxidative or corrosive environments over durations sufficient to reach steady-state oxidation; behaviors at lower temperatures or in markedly different microstructures may differ.
generation.uncertainty: Quantitative details such as the exact diffusion rates, oxide thicknesses, and the contribution of mixed oxide systems (e.g., synergistic effects with Cr2O3) remain uncertain and require further experimental quantification.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize a series of CrFeCoNiX alloys with X = Al, Si, and Mn using identical processing routes to achieve similar solid-solution microstructures. Expose each alloy to a controlled oxidative or corrosive atmosphere at a temperature above 900 °C (for example, 950 °C) for a set duration (e.g., 50 hours). Characterize the surface oxide layers using scanning electron microscopy (SEM) with cross-sectional imaging, X-ray diffraction (XRD) for phase identification, and adhesion/spallation tests.
measurements: Oxide scale thickness and uniformity via SEM cross-sectional imaging
Phase composition and crystallinity of the oxide layer using XRD
Adhesion strength and spallation resistance using mechanical pull-off or scratch tests
Mass gain measurements over time to evaluate oxidation kinetics
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the alloys with X = Al or Si do not exhibit significantly more coherent, slow-growing, and adherent oxide scales compared to the Mn-containing alloy under identical high-temperature exposure, then the hypothesis—that the oxidation and diffusion characteristics of the X element govern the formation of a protective oxide scale—is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: In CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys, the formation and persistence of a stable, coherent protective oxide layer at temperatures above 900 °C is governed by the degree of lattice parameter matching between the protective oxide (enriched in the X element with high oxide‐forming ability) and the underlying alloy. A close lattice match minimizes interfacial strain and defect nucleation, leading to a coherent, adherent oxide layer, while a larger mismatch results in unstable, cracking or spalling oxides.
drafts.material_initial_state: CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloy (with X = Si, Mn, or Al) in a single- or multiphase solid-solution state.
drafts.intervention: Exposure to high-temperature (>900 °C) oxidative or corrosive atmosphere under controlled conditions.
drafts.conditions: Tests conducted in controlled furnaces using air or simulated corrosive gas mixtures at temperatures above 900 °C, with dwell times sufficient for oxide growth (e.g., 10–100 hours). Baseline comparison involves similar alloys lacking the specific lattice-matching X element or containing elements that lead to larger mismatch.
drafts.structural_mediator: The lattice mismatch (i.e., the interfacial misfit strain) between the protective oxide phase and the underlying alloy substrate.
drafts.mechanism: Addition of X (Si, Mn, or Al) influences the composition and structure of the oxide formed. When the oxide that preferentially forms (e.g., SiO2 or Al2O3) has a lattice parameter close to that of the substrate, it creates a coherent interface with low interfacial energy, reducing the likelihood of crack initiation and spallation. Conversely, if the oxide and substrate are poorly lattice-matched, increased interfacial strain promotes the development of unstable, cracked, or spalled scales.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Alloys where X leads to a well-matched oxide scale will show a persistent, coherent, and adherent oxide layer during high-temperature exposure. In contrast, alloys with significant lattice mismatch will develop unstable oxide layers that crack or spall, leading to accelerated degradation.
drafts.baseline: Alloys without the beneficial X addition or with alternative X elements that do not achieve good lattice matching serve as the control, exhibiting unstable oxide scales under the same exposure conditions.
drafts.boundary: This hypothesis applies to single- or multiphase solid-solution CrFeCoNiX alloys subjected to oxidative or corrosive atmospheres at temperatures above 900 °C. It is valid as long as the protective oxidation process and microstructural changes are governed primarily by lattice matching.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of CrFeCoNiX alloys with controlled microstructures and varying X elements (Si, Mn, and Al). Expose samples to a controlled oxidative atmosphere at temperatures above 900 °C for different durations (e.g., 10, 50, 100 hours). Analyze the oxide scales for lattice parameters, coherence at the oxide/alloy interface, and mechanical integrity (e.g., via SEM, TEM, XRD, and adhesion tests). Complement these analyses with quantitative assessments of interfacial strain.
measurements: Lattice parameter measurements of both the substrate and the oxide layer (XRD, TEM)
Interfacial structure and coherence (TEM, high-resolution SEM)
Oxide scale adherence and spallation behavior (adhesion tests, mechanical cycling)
Kinetic data of oxide scale growth (mass gain measurements)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if alloys predicted to have low lattice mismatch (and thus expected to maintain a coherent oxide) instead show oxide scales that are unstable, cracked, or spalled to a similar degree as the baseline. Similarly, if alloys expected to form unstable oxides due to high lattice mismatch are found to possess a stable, coherent oxide layer, the hypothesis does not hold.

drafts.hypothesis: In CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys, the formation and persistence of a stable, coherent protective oxide layer above 900 °C is governed by the ability of alloying elements (specifically Si and Al) to promote the surface segregation and reaction of Cr with Si or Al, forming slow-growing, adherent oxides such as SiO2 or Al2O3 (in synergy with Cr2O3). In contrast, when Mn is the X element, its tendency to form volatile or non-adherent oxides leads to unstable surface scales that crack or spall.
drafts.material_initial_state: CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys (single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state) with X = Si, Mn, or Al.
drafts.intervention: Expose the alloys to temperatures above 900 °C under oxidative or corrosive atmospheres.
drafts.conditions: Isothermal exposure above 900 °C in controlled oxidative/corrosive atmospheres (e.g., air or humid environments) for set durations, with alloys prepared to have comparable microstructures except for the substitutional element (Si, Mn, or Al).
drafts.structural_mediator: The formation of an oxide scale that is structurally coherent and adherent to the underlying metallic substrate, mediating stress accommodation and limiting scale cracking/spallation.
drafts.mechanism: Si and Al additions enhance the segregation of these elements to the surface where they react with chromium to form a mixed protective oxide layer (e.g., SiO2/Cr2O3 or Al2O3/Cr2O3) with superior adhesion and mismatch strain accommodation. Conversely, Mn promotes formation of oxides that are more prone to volatility or poor adhesion, resulting in surface instability.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Alloys with Si or Al will develop and maintain a coherent, adherent protective oxide layer during high-temperature exposure, whereas alloys with Mn will tend to form unstable, cracked, or spalled oxide scales.
drafts.baseline: Comparison against a defined baseline of CrFeCoNiMn alloy under identical high-temperature oxidative/corrosive exposure.
drafts.boundary: Valid for CrFeCoNiX alloys in single-phase or well-characterized multiphase solid-solution states, exposed above 900 °C in oxidative or corrosive (e.g., humid air) environments; effects outside this temperature range or in fundamentally different microstructures are not covered.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of CrFeCoNiX alloys with controlled substitution for X (i.e., Si, Mn, Al). Expose each alloy to isothermal conditions above 900 °C in a controlled oxidative or corrosive atmosphere for a fixed duration. Characterize the surface oxide layers for phase composition, thickness, adhesion, and microstructural coherence using techniques such as SEM, XRD, and EDS mapping.
measurements: Oxide scale thickness and morphology via SEM
Crystallographic analysis of oxide phases using XRD
Elemental segregation profiles via EDS or SIMS
Adhesion and spallation resistance assessments through thermal cycling or mechanical testing
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If alloys containing Si or Al fail to form a coherent, adherent oxide scale or if the Mn-containing alloy shows oxide scale stability and adhesion comparable to the Si/Al alloys under identical conditions, the proposed mechanism (that surface segregation of Si/Al promotes the formation of protective oxides) is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: In CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys, the formation and long‐term stability of a protective oxide layer at temperatures above 900 °C is primarily controlled by the diffusion behavior and oxide‐forming character of the X element. When X is Al or Si, their slower diffusion and tendency to form strong, adherent oxides (Al2O3 or SiO2) leads to a coherent, low-strain barrier; in contrast, when X is Mn, its higher diffusivity and formation of less stable, volatile manganese oxides result in poorly adhering scales that crack and spall.
drafts.material_initial_state: CrFeCoNiX alloy in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state
drafts.intervention: Exposure to an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere at temperatures above 900 °C
drafts.conditions: Isothermal or near-isothermal conditions above 900 °C under controlled oxidative or corrosive environments
drafts.structural_mediator: The nature and spatial distribution of the surface oxide phases (e.g., a continuous Al2O3 or SiO2 layer versus discontinuous Mn-rich oxides) and the interfacial coherency between the oxide scale and the alloy substrate
drafts.mechanism: When X = Al or Si, the relatively slow diffusion and strong bonding energies promote the nucleation and growth of a dense, slowly thickening oxide layer with low internal stress, leading to excellent adhesion. Conversely, for X = Mn, rapid outward diffusion and formation of volatile oxides cause rapid scale growth, larger stress accumulation, and subsequent cracking or spallation of the oxide layer.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Alloys with X = Al or Si will develop a thin, stable, and coherent oxide layer with minimal spallation over extended high-temperature exposure; alloys with X = Mn will exhibit thicker, irregular oxide scales that crack and spall, undermining protective performance.
drafts.baseline: A reference CrFeCoNi alloy lacking the X element (or with X = Mn, known to form less protective oxides) serves as the control to compare oxide scale coherence and durability.
drafts.boundary: This hypothesis is applicable for high-temperature exposures (T > 900 °C) and may differ in behavior at lower temperatures or under different thermal cycling regimes; variations between single-phase and multiphase microstructures may introduce additional complexities.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate series of CrFeCoNiX alloys where X is varied among Al, Si, and Mn (keeping other parameters constant) in both single-phase and multiphase microstructures. Expose these samples to a controlled oxidative/corrosive environment at temperatures above 900 °C for extended durations, with and without thermal cycling.
measurements: Examine oxide scale morphology and continuity using SEM and TEM
Quantify oxide scale thickness and spallation rates through weight change measurements
Determine element diffusion profiles near the oxide/alloy interface via EDS or SIMS
Assess adhesion strength of the oxide layer using mechanical pull-off or scratch tests
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If alloys with X = Al or Si develop oxide scales that exhibit cracking, spallation, or discontinuities similar to those observed in alloys with X = Mn, or if alloys with X = Mn unexpectedly form stable, coherent oxide scales comparable to those formed with Al or Si, then the hypothesis—that the X element’s diffusion and oxide formation behavior governs protective oxide scale stability—is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: In CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys, the ability to form a stable, coherent protective oxide layer at temperatures above 900 °C is primarily governed by the oxidation kinetics of the X element. When X is Al, the alloy preferentially forms a slow-growing, adherent Al2O3 scale because aluminum diffuses more slowly and its oxide is thermodynamically more stable than volatile chromium oxides. In contrast, when X is Si or Mn, the more rapid outward diffusion of Cr (and its tendency to form volatile or poorly adherent oxides such as CrO3) leads to the formation of unstable oxide layers that crack or spall.
drafts.material_initial_state: CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloy in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state (with X = Al, Si, or Mn)
drafts.intervention: Exposure of the alloy to an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere at temperatures above 900 °C
drafts.conditions: High-temperature exposure (e.g., 900–1100 °C) in air or oxidative/corrosive environments for extended durations (tens of hours), with the alloy initially in a well-homogenized solid-solution microstructure
drafts.structural_mediator: The nature and coherence of the oxide scale formed at the alloy surface, which is mediated by the diffusion rates and oxidation kinetics of the constituent elements (particularly those of Al versus Cr, Si, and Mn) and by the uniform elemental distribution inherent in high-entropy alloys
drafts.mechanism: The formation of a protective scale depends on the balance between the outward diffusion of oxide-forming elements and inward oxygen diffusion. In alloys where the X element is Al, the slower growth kinetics and high thermodynamic stability of Al2O3 yield a dense, adherent oxide layer that remains coherent. When X is Si or Mn, rapid Cr diffusion and the associated formation of volatile or less-protective chromium oxides lead to scale cracking and spallation. Thus, the inherent oxidation behavior of the X element determines the quality of the scale despite the high configurational entropy that promotes uniformity.
drafts.predicted_outcome: CrFeCoNiAl alloys will develop a slow-growing, coherent Al2O3 layer that effectively protects the substrate at >900 °C, whereas CrFeCoNiSi and CrFeCoNiMn alloys will form oxide scales that are prone to cracking and spallation due to faster Cr diffusion and oxide volatility.
drafts.baseline: Comparative performance is established against CrFeCoNiX alloys where X is Si or Mn, which are expected to exhibit non-protective, unstable oxide layers under the same high-temperature oxidative/corrosive conditions.
drafts.boundary: The hypothesis applies to conditions above 900 °C in oxidative or corrosive atmospheres, during exposures of sufficient duration (e.g., tens of hours) such that differences in oxide growth kinetics and scale adherence can be observed.

Expose samples from each series to a controlled oxidative or corrosive environment at a temperature above 900 °C (e.g., 950 °C) for a set duration (e.g., 50 hours). Use SEM (with cross-sectional analysis), XRD, and adhesion tests to characterize the oxide scale morphology, composition, and resistance to spallation.
measurements: Oxide scale thickness and uniformity (via SEM cross-section imaging)
Phase composition of the oxide layer (via XRD)
Adhesion and integrity of the oxide scale (via spallation tests or scratch tests)
Mass gain measurements over time to evaluate oxidation kinetics
